title: Organic practical techniques
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: OR27#t2 term and clue written for the game; OR27#t3 term and clue written for the game; OR27#t1 term and clue written for the game; OR27#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: OR27#N.4, OR27#N.8, OR27#N.11, OR27#N.14.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Distillation
items.clue: Separates liquids by boiling point, using a condenser that slopes down to a receiver.

items.label: Separating funnel
items.clue: Tap apparatus for two liquids that do not mix: the denser lower layer is run off first.

items.label: Reflux
items.clue: Long heating with a vertical condenser, so vapour condenses and drips back into the flask.

items.label: Recrystallisation
items.clue: Dissolve a crude solid in the minimum of hot solvent, cool slowly, then filter under reduced pressure.

questions.stem: A student wants to make propanal from propan-1-ol using acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Which method gives the most propanal?

options.text: Heat the alcohol under reflux with excess oxidant for an hour, then distil the mixture.
Heat the alcohol under reflux with a small amount of oxidant, then distil.
Distil the alcohol first, then add the oxidant to the distillate.
Add the oxidant slowly to warm alcohol and distil off propanal as it forms.

questions.explanation: Propanal (bp 48 °C) boils lower than propan-1-ol (97 °C), so it distils out before it can be oxidised further.

questions.stem: A student shakes a crude organic product with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution in a separating funnel. Why must the tap be opened often?

options.text: To let air in, so that the two layers can separate cleanly from each other.
To release carbon dioxide made as acid reacts with the hydrogencarbonate.
To let water vapour escape, which dries the organic layer.
To stop the organic layer from boiling as the neutralisation reaction heats it.

questions.explanation: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂. The gas builds up pressure that could force out the stopper.

questions.stem: Pure aspirin melts at 136 °C. A student's recrystallised aspirin melts over the range 126–131 °C. What does this show?

options.text: It is pure: melting below 136 °C shows that no aspirin decomposed.
It is impure: the impurity must be a substance that melts at 126 °C.
It is impure: impurities lower the melting point and widen the range.
It is pure: every pure solid melts gradually over a range of about 5 °C.

questions.explanation: Low and broad (126–131 °C) means impure. Recrystallise again and re-measure.

questions.stem: A student makes 1-bromobutane (bp 102 °C, density 1.27 g cm⁻³) from butan-1-ol (bp 118 °C). The crude product contains water, acid and some unreacted alcohol. Which purification is best?

options.text: Keep the upper layer, since organic liquids float on water; dry it, then distil at 100–104 °C.
Keep the lower layer; wash with NaHCO₃(aq), venting; dry; distil at 100–104 °C.
Dry the crude mixture with anhydrous MgSO₄ first, then wash it with water and distil.
Keep the lower layer, dry it, then collect everything that distils below 118 °C.

questions.explanation: Density puts the product at the bottom; NaHCO₃ removes acid; the salt removes water; distilling near 102 °C leaves the alcohol (118 °C) behind.
